items.text: First Session, Forty-ninth Parliament, 2008-10
Parliamentary Debates
(HANSARD)
Thursday, 25 November 2010
(Week 61, Volume 669)
Published under the authority of the House of Representatives—2010
THURSDAY, 25 NOVEMBER 2010
MOTIONS—
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15807
THURSDAY, 25 NOVEMBER 2010
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
MOTIONS
Pike River Mine, West Coast—Tragedy
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister:
I move, That the House mark the tragic loss of life that has occurred at the Pike River
coalmine; express its deepest sympathy to the family and the friends of the men who
died; thank the rescue teams and support teams who were so willingly prepared to help;
and acknowledge the profound impact on the communities that this disaster has
affected. Today is a day for mourning and re membering. At 3.45 on the afternoon of
Friday, 19 November, a large underground expl osion tore through the Pike River mine,
46 kilometres north-east of Gr eymouth on the West Coast. Th irty-one men were in the
mine at the time of the explosion. Tw o escaped to safety; 29 others—24 New
Zealanders, two Australians, two Britons, and one South African—did not emerge from
the mine. For 5 days we hoped they could still be alive. But at 2.37 p.m. yesterday a
second explosion ripped through the mine, extinguishing all hope of their survival.
The death of these men is a tragedy for their families, their workmates and friends,
their community, and our nation. Our thoughts are with the miners’ families in their
immense grief and loss. As the Prime Minister said to them yesterday: “Though we
cannot possibly feel this pain as you do, we  have you in our hearts and our thoughts.”
On behalf of the people of New Zealand, this  House extends its sympathies and support
to the miners’ parents, wives, girlfriends, siblings, and mates. It is important, in
particular, that the children who have lost their fathers will remember them with pride
and know that their loss was felt by a nation.
Support and condolences have flowed in from throughout the country and around the
world. This tragedy reminds us again of the history of Austra lia and New Zealand
standing together in adversity. The Australian mining industry has generously
contributed technical expertise, and a flag flies at half mast on the ANZAC Bridge in
Sydney.
We thank all of those who have worked so hard on the attempted rescue of these
men. From the moment of the first expl osion, they have spent every waking hour
tirelessly working, searching for a way to bring these men home alive. We acknowledge
their professionalism at a time of enormous  frustration. We also acknowledge all those
who have given their time and energy to support the families. Much more will be asked
of them in the days to come.
The next step now is to make the mine as safe as possible, so that the men’s bodies
can be recovered. It is also  natural and appropriate that New Zealanders are seeking
answers to how this disaster occurred. Fam ilies want certainty about  the events leading
up to their loved ones’ deaths, and we all need to know how such a disaster can be
prevented in the future. Cabinet will confirm the details of a commission of inquiry at
its next meeting on Monday, along with an y other inquiries th at may be deemed
appropriate.
Today we also acknowledge the sense of loss felt by all New Zealanders who have
watched the story of the Pike River miners  unfold. Each passing day of this tragedy
made the hopes and frustrations of the West  Coast community and the miners’ families
our hopes and frustrations. These are me n whose names we did not know, but we
instinctively recognised their qua lities collectively as the be st of ours. These were men
15808 Motions 25 Nov 2010
who knew the strain and satis faction of physical work, a nd who lived in a community
where teamwork, hard work, and practical skill are respected. They were breadwinners
for their families and earners for their community. They died not fighting a war in a
strange land, nor taking undue risks; they di ed, shockingly, going to work. They were
ordinary people who died in extraordinary and perhaps horrible circumstances. Their
numbers are no consolation to the grief of each  individual family. That is the pain of
each family alone. But the scale and the horror of this tragedy have dragged us all to the
entrance of the Pike River mine, and today we stand there together with the families and
the West Coast community, contemplating wh at might have happened in the darkness.
Who among us did not hope that the qualities of these men, which we regard as the best
of our own qualities, would tr iumph over the odds and lead them into the light? It was
not to be.
As the tragedy passes, it is our hope that  the families and communities can be held
together by the toughness, the comradeship, the resilience, and the commitment to the
common good that we all share with those w ho are lost. The darkness took their lives,
but it cannot take the love th at these men had for their families and their mates, and nor
can it take our respect for them. May they rest in peace.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The Labour Opposition joins
all parties in this House in sending our sympathy to the families and friends of the 29
men who perished in the Pike River Coal mi ne disaster yesterday. We are also thinking
of the people of the West Coast who have woke n this morning to the reality of the loss,
knowing that all hope of life has been extinguished.
Not a day goes by that we do not hear or read of a tragedy somewhere in the world
from natural or human causes—earthquakes to floods, famine to fire—and we watch the
passing parade of pictures on our television sets . We feel sad at their loss and we shake
our heads at the enormity of their tragedy, but nothing hurts like the death of your own.
Twenty-nine men have died, and although fi ve of them are from other countries—
Scotland, Australia, and South Africa—they now lie alongside our men and they too are
now New Zealanders.
There will be very few people in New Zealand today who do not feel a sense of loss
and deep sadness as we look at  the faces of the family members, the rescuers, the
community leaders, and the clergy, all grief-stri cken at their loss and frustrated at their
inability to save those lives. As the headlin es in our newspaper said today, it is “Our
darkest hour”. So many words have already be en said and written over the past 6 days,
and no doubt many more will follow. Eventuall y, the stories of this  tragedy will also
become part of the West Coast legend.
On Friday the Mayor of Grey District, Tony Kokshoorn, who has shown incredible
leadership, said that there was a little bit of the West Coast in all of us. I think he is
right. But there is a little bit of the coalmine r in many of us, as well. My old dad started
his working life at 14 years of age in the Owen River mine, 13 miles north of
Murchison. His dad worked in the mine, t oo. And his dad before him worked in the
Denniston mine, where he broke his back in a mining accident. And his dad was a miner
from Jarrow, County Durham, who came to New Zealand for a better life—and my
generation got that better life. That will be a familiar story for thousands of New
Zealanders whose family grew out of a mi ning tradition on the We st Coast, or in
Southland, Huntly, or Waihī.
When most of us think of working in a coalmine, we think of dirt and dust and
darkness, hard labour, and da nger. But for those who go down  the mines it is a way of
life. Few other jobs build the sense of brotherhood and loyalty to each other that miners
have. The West Coast reputati on of stoic, strong fighters ar ises out of that mining
tradition. Now all that strength of character and fighting spirit are going to be needed in
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15809
the days ahead. As John Crowley, a West Coaster writing in the Dominion Post  said
today, “what will tomorrow bring … It will br ing a heavy blanket of abject sadness.”,
until the region rises again from  this devastating experience. It will rise again, and they
will not be alone.
This morning I was talking to Rick Barker. He is a boy from Rūnanga, who has spent
the last 5 days in Greymouth. He said what a close-knit commun ity it is. In one street in
Rūnanga, Ranfurly Street, two grieving mothers live just a short distance apart. Many
others in that street are connected to the mi ners who died. Rick sa id there have been 5
days of dread, 5 days of hope, 5 days of c ourage, and 5 days of great leadership, but
now is the time to mourn, and to focus on retrieving the bodies of the men so that there
can be closure for their families. Then there will be a time to find out what went wrong.
May they rest in peace.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: A speech like this is normally given by one of our co-
leaders, and I want to begin by expressing my thanks to Metiria and Russel for giving
me the opportunity to speak on this tragedy today and to express our profound sorrow. I
live the closest to the mine of anyone in this Parliament. When I spoke earl ier this week
about every family and every household in and around Greymouth being connected to at
least one of the men who is trapped in the mine, I include my own in that. One of my
partner’s relations was killed in the Strongm an Mine disaster in 1967. That tragedy has
echoed down the years, through our family and through the community. Now the name
of Pike River joins that te rrible toll of Strongman, Dobson, Brunner, and many other
disasters. Those who were bereaved by these previous disasters will feel afresh their
own pain but will also know best of all the anguish a nd grief now being experienced by
the families and friends of the 29 men killed.
When I spoke on Tuesday I expressed the fervent hope that the men would be
brought home. That is still my fervent hope . Families need the bodies of their loved
ones to come home so that they may prope rly grieve, and I know that that is well
understood and that no effort will be spared, nor should it, to do this.
I want to again express my and the Green Party’s sincerest thanks and admiration for
the work done by Tony Kokshoorn, Gary Know les and the police, the other emergency
services and Mines Rescue, the district he alth board and its staff, the New Zealand
Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union, the Red Cross, the
churches of Greymouth, and everyone else who has been involved in providing support.
I want to express my personal gratitude to  other members of this House—those who
have been helping out directly on the Coast, but also everyone else. I feel that when I
return home this afternoon, I will be carrying with me the support and well-wishes of
this whole House. I will single out Peter Whittall. I know Peter pe rsonally, but I will
take this public opportunity  to convey the Green Part y’s thanks, our enormous
sympathy, but also our tremendous respec t for the integrity, responsibility, and
compassion that he has unfailingly shown. I am sure that that is a feeling shared by the
nation.
There is a memorial to those lost in the Brunner Mine disast er in the road leading out
of Greymouth up towards Pike River. It carries an inscription from the New Zealand
Tablet from 3 April 1896: “While the wido ws and orphans were watching with
heartbroken anxiety at the pit mouth for the result of the rescue work, all New Zealand
seemed to stand by and share the grief of the bereaved ones.” This is a loss being felt by
a whole country. When we consider the deva station and emptiness that we feel, we
know that this is nothing compared with the utter loss suffered by the bereaved families.
Our hearts go out to you. If we could shar e your burden, we would do it, but we cannot.
We will sup
port you in any way that we can, and we will remember them.
15810 Motions 25 Nov 2010

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: It is with deep and overwhelming sadness
that I rise today on behalf of the ACT Party to join with all members of this House to
offer our heartfelt sympathy and our support to  the families and to the loved ones of the
Pike River coalminers whose lives have b een so tragically taken away. Words cannot
even begin to express the sorrow we f eel at the profound loss of 29 good men, who
were loved by their community and by their fa milies. We are also well aware that the
deep sorrow that we feel now is only a frac tion of that being experienced on the West
Coast.
The people of Greymouth possess an immense strength of characte r. We have seen
your courage and your determination time and time again. We have seen you face
adversity head on. The days to come will be  incredibly difficult , both emotionally and
physically, but we know that you will come  through this and your community will
become stronger.
All New Zealanders are united in grief today and will never ever forget the loss of
these 29 miners. These men were part of the backbone of New Zealand: family men,
working men; men who kissed their wives, their parents, and th eir children goodbye as
they left for work on Friday, never once imagining that they would not be coming
home. I cannot begin to comprehend how those families must be feeling right now.
I too wish to thank the entire rescue t eam and all those who offered assistance,
advice, support, and expertise. We know that  there is still much work to be done, but
your efforts will be of invaluable assistance and comfort in this time of need.
I say thank you to Peter Whittall, Chief Executive of Pike River Coal. Thank you for
your leadership, your courage, your honest y, and your humanity. I know that all New
Zealanders will continue to support you and all your staff in the days and weeks ahead. I
know that the job and the decisions you have ahead of you to ensure that Pike River
Coal remains on the West Coast, and to ensure the employment of miners and staff, will
be difficult but it is of critical importance.
As Minister of Local Government, let me  pay tribute to councillor Milton John
Osborne, 54, of Ng āhere, who was one of the 29 in th e mine at the time of Friday’s
explosion. Milton was serving his second te rm on the Grey District Council as a
representative for the eastern ward where he was elected unopposed. He was also a
contractor at the Pike River mine. Grey District Council Chief Executive, Paul
Pretorius, said that Milton was highly respected for his council work. He took a wide
interest in council issues. Th e area he represented was very close to him. Milton had a
special concern for the farming issues in Ng āhere, and he represen ted the farmers with
conviction. Milton always looked at the merits  of each case and carefully considered
things, always coming very well prepared to council meetings. His input was ever
thoughtful and he also included the lighter side, while always making perfect sense.
Milton was a big friendly guy with a great se nse of humour. He could come up with a
joke at the most appropriate and, indeed, th e most inappropriate times. He lived his life
without apology. He was a caring father and a good husband. He and his wife were
great friends. He was respected, he was valu ed, and he was loved as a member of the
council. I would like to quote Paul’s fina l comment verbatim: “Milton epitomises the

items.speaker: West Coast
items.text: he was a good bastard.”
I also wish to acknowledge  and thank the Mayor of Greymouth, Tony Kokshoorn,
who has been the face of the community dur ing this difficult and gut-wrenching time.
Tony’s courage, support, and leadership gave strength to the families and friends who
live in this close-knit community. I offer you my support and strength.
As Associate Minister of Education, I also  recognise the work of the Ministry of
Education’s traumatic incident team. The team has worked ti relessly to support staff in
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15811
schools and early childhood education services in the area so that children can maintain
the rhythm of their lives during a time of great uncertainty and sorrow.
Mining is a way of life on the West Coast,  and in Greymouth especially. For many
families, mining is more than just a liveli hood; it is a tradition. On e could say it is in
their blood. It is for this reason that we cannot allow mining to cease on the West Coast;
rather we must find out how this happened a nd we must see what lessons we can learn
from it. Although it is difficult today to see beyond the sorrow, may looking back in
memory help comfort you tomorrow. Rest in peace. God bless their souls.

items.speaker: Hon JIM ANDERTON
items.text: Like all New Zealanders, I am
deeply saddened by the loss of the 29 mi ners in Greymouth, and my thoughts and
prayers are with the loved ones who are left behind.
As a nation, and as a House I am sure, we have clung on to a glimmer of hope in the
past 6 days. With every passing hour we ha ve put our faith in the possibility of a
miracle. Fears over entering the mine safely, which had been such a concern to
Superintendent Gary Knowles, were well justified when th e second explosion occurred
yesterday. He and Pike River Coal Chief Executive Peter Whittall have shown calm,
intelligent leadership and great strength at a difficult time. No praise is high enough for
all of those who were part of the plans to secure the rescue of these men. Hope,
however, for the 29 men trapped down the Pi ke River mine disappeared yesterday
afternoon.
This event has, of course, been a tragedy for the West Coast and its community and,
needless to say, for the whole of New Zeala nd. It brought back some sad memories to
many who have, unfortunately, been in this space before. Mining is an iconic industry
on the West Coast, but that does not mean, however, that the rest of us have no
responsibility for ensuring that such a tragedy does not happen again. We must refuse to
accept that any of the deaths are a necessary cost of mining. It is a responsibility of all
of us, from mine operators to  the Government and this Parliament, to take steps to
strengthen mine safety so that the safety of all our miners is our No. 1 concern.
Pike River is a modern, state-of-the-art mine with, presumably, all of the latest safety
technology. But that did not sa ve the lives of the 29 men we lost yesterday. The new
mine was on the same coal seam as the mine in Brunner where 65 men were killed by
choking gas in 1896. It echoed th e Strongman mine explosion, which killed 19 miners
in 1967. And there have been, even as recently as last year, many other similar disasters
in other countries. How many more deaths mu st we experience in this industry before
we ask some very serious questions about the vi ability of this type of mine? It will be
the best possible tribute to those who di ed if we carefully examine the most
comprehensive safety measures possible before we put any more miners in harm’s way.
Since colonisation, the West Coast has had a long history in mining. The risk of
mining has always been faced by miners and, as  a consequence, their families. Today is
a time to reflect on the human tragedy of th is latest mining disast er, but these precious
lost lives must be treasured th rough the efforts of all of us to see that this kind of
catastrophe does not occur again.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: There are, thankfully, only a few
awful tragedies in the life of a nation that ar e so powerful in their impact, so searing on
the emotions, that we all stop still, frozen in time as it were for that moment, and reflect
upon what has happened, what its impact is going to be, and what its impact on us as a
nation has been. Although it would be infelicitous to make comparisons, I can think of a
few in my own lifetime to which the tragic events at Pike River must now be added. It is
not just, awful as it is, the death of 29 mine rs in horrific circumstances; this was an
event that stopped a nation. We all felt fo r those miners—desperately—and even more
so for their families and loved ones, their friends, their neighb ours, and their colleagues.
15812 Motions 25 Nov 2010
Every time Peter Whittall appeared on television to provide an update we could see and
feel his pain and his genuine sense of wanti ng desperately to bring those men out alive,
and we were with him. Yesterday’s events dashed whatever remaining hopes there were
in that regard, and now a country, a region, and individual families deal with the
consequences.
I guess that for those families there will be the awful shock of adjusting to what has
happened. There will be the consolation of a tight-knit community and the love of a
nation all around them. But, sadly, that is passing. Once the memorial services have
been held, and once life starts to pick up its inevitable threads again, their pain will
endure and their grief will carry on. The r eal challenge for all of us in this
compassionate society is about their ongoing support and their ongoing place in our
collective heart, as we struggle to overcome the consequences of this tragedy.
It bites deep. It is not just a case of thinking about th e West Coast and what has
happened there. Earlier this morning I was vi siting Inland Revenue Department staff in
Christchurch, partly in the wake of the events that they have suffered following the
Christchurch earthquake, only to be inform ed that one of the staff members in
Christchurch is the mother of one of thos e lost in the mine. So we have people who
have gone through a different set of em otions, following an earthquake, coming
together to get over those, to now be faced with another tragedy in their midst. This
must surely be New Zealand’s annus horribilis.
At this time our words are inadequate, however well meant, and our gestures,
however well meant, will not be  enough. Our challeng e as a people as we stand still so
numbed by this shock, so awestruck by what  has happened, is to never forget those
families, to do what we can to assist them materially and otherwise right now and into
the future, and to pay them the ultimate c ourtesy of finding out what happened, what
lessons can be learnt, and what steps can be taken to prevent any form of repetition at a
future date.
Much has been said about the heart a nd soul of the miners, and I acknowledge
particularly the comments from my collea gue Mr Hide regarding Milton Osborne, who
as I said the other day had been a candi date for United Future at the 2005 general
election. I acknowledge the stor ies we are hearing about so  many of the other miners—
their contributions to life well beyond their working careers, to their families, their
communities, and their sports . I acknowledge also the hopes that are now diminished
and will never be achieved, and the aspirations unmet.
This is an occasion where we all figurative ly want to give those suffering people one
giant hug of support. I suppose the only thing we can now hope for is that the bodies are
recovered quickly, that there can be closur e through the memorial services, and that
those who suffered and died so unnecessarily can at last rest in peace.

[Cease the winds from the west, cease the winds from the south, let the breezes blow
over the land, let the breezes blow over the ocean. Let the red-tipped dawn come with a
sharpened air, a touch of frost, a promise of a glorious day. Behold the sneeze of life!
Oh disaster, oh deaths, oh calami ties of the moment, oh mighty t ōtara trees of the
forest, those of you taken by the Great H and of Death, sleep there, rest there, and
slumber on. You went into the bowels of mother  Earth to carry out your responsibilities
that would ensure sustenance for the ch ildren, grandchildren, yourselves, and your
friends, but never to return to the world of brightness and enlightenment.
This is why I am standing here, following up the circumstance of today’s speeches,
oh old and young ones, paying tribute to you hi dden there from the world of brightness
and enlightenment; instead, you are there in  the bowels of mother Earth, waiting,
waiting, and waiting. Meanwhile, on the surface of mother Earth, the nation is waiting,
as well—waiting, waiting, and waiting. But in the end, you are not coming back alive
into the arms of your families, as before. You were warriors in your time, worked hard,
gave advice, nurtured your fam ilies, but are not returning alive. This is the reason why
we are grieving inside, because you are lying there, conceale d from us in the bowels of
mother Earth. Here is the country and the wo rld in mourning for you. Rest in peace,
rest in peace, rest in peace.
The nation weeps—Mā ori, non-M āori, children, adults, elderly womenfolk, elderly
menfolk— this, then, is the nation that mourns  for you; rest peacefully, rest peacefully,
rest peacefully. We have hear d stories about you in the prim e of your life, during your
life on the land. The country is proud of you. Indeed, yes! It is not as though you
reached the pinnacles of the country, adorned the walls of Parliament House. No, not at
all! But in the hearts of your families, y ou reached the right levels. You cannot ignore
that. Not at all. So today, colleagues, ther e is only one statement, one thought, and one
spirit; it is about you who are no longer here, gone. You have reached the very pinnacle
of the universe. Sleep, rest, and lie there.
To the people of the country, let me say this: leave them there to rest and slumber. I
come back to us, the world of the living, to  us throughout our House: greetings to you,
and greetings to us all. Lest we forget, as others before me alluded to, the country’s
services made every attempt to rescue these men. We must acknowledge their efforts, in
the full knowledge that they were heart-bro ken, as well, because they were close work
compatriots and friends to each other. We need to recognise this. My part is merely to
follow up on the acknowledgments by thes e ones who spoke before me. The real
problem is that the outcome was not what we all wanted.
As I was making my way home after completing some work relating to Parliament
last night, I was thinking to myself: if I am grieving like th is for 29 people, how did the
country react to a war in past years? Look about you. There are th e memorial symbols
commemorating those who fell. This is a mere 29, and the country is grief-stricken. How
I feel sorry for us all. They are the ones who died. At Dobson, four died; At Strongman,
15; at Cave Creek, 14; so the heart grieves. Only one company of men died today, so let
them rest there. All I am simply saying to each and every one of you in the House is to
allow them to rest there. My call to the fa milies, the region, and the country in grief is
for us to be staunch, to stand shoulder to shoulder, hand in hand, and support those
who are in grief now so that they do not feel alone and anxious. We must make them
stronger, because they mirror us in our grief. So greetings to you throughout the House,
and greetings to you all.
Show me
Your cross
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15815
Let it shine there in the darkness
I look to thee
In life and death,
Let me abide with thee.

Your cross
Let it shine there in the darkness
I look to thee
In life and death,
Let me abide with thee.
Amen.]
Members joined in the singing of the waiata.

[Let the spirituality of our ancestors settle upon us. They were the ones who set down

items.text: Honourable members, with our thoughts and prayers firmly focused

plain_text:
First Session, Forty-ninth Parliament, 2008-10 
 
 
 
 
Parliamentary Debates 
(HANSARD) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Thursday, 25 November 2010 
(Week 61, Volume 669) 
 
 
 
 
WELLINGTON, NEW ZEALAND 
Published under the authority of the House of Representatives—2010 
 
 
 
THURSDAY, 25 NOVEMBER 2010 
TABLE OF CONTENTS 
MOTIONS— 
Pike River Mine, West Coast—Tragedy .........................................................15807 
 
 
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15807 
THURSDAY, 25 NOVEMBER 2010 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
Pike River Mine, West Coast—Tragedy 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister) on behalf of the Prime Minister: 
I move, That the House mark the tragic loss of life that has occurred at the Pike River 
coalmine; express its deepest sympathy to the family and the friends of the men who 
died; thank the rescue teams and support teams who were so willingly prepared to help; 
and acknowledge the profound impact on the communities that this disaster has 
affected. Today is a day for mourning and re membering. At 3.45 on the afternoon of 
Friday, 19 November, a large underground expl osion tore through the Pike River mine, 
46 kilometres north-east of Gr eymouth on the West Coast. Th irty-one men were in the 
mine at the time of the explosion. Tw o escaped to safety; 29 others—24 New 
Zealanders, two Australians, two Britons, and one South African—did not emerge from 
the mine. For 5 days we hoped they could still be alive. But at 2.37 p.m. yesterday a 
second explosion ripped through the mine, extinguishing all hope of their survival.  
The death of these men is a tragedy for their families, their workmates and friends, 
their community, and our nation. Our thoughts are with the miners’ families in their 
immense grief and loss. As the Prime Minister said to them yesterday: “Though we 
cannot possibly feel this pain as you do, we  have you in our hearts and our thoughts.” 
On behalf of the people of New Zealand, this  House extends its sympathies and support 
to the miners’ parents, wives, girlfriends, siblings, and mates. It is important, in 
particular, that the children who have lost their fathers will remember them with pride 
and know that their loss was felt by a nation.  
Support and condolences have flowed in from throughout the country and around the 
world. This tragedy reminds us again of the history of Austra lia and New Zealand 
standing together in adversity. The Australian mining industry has generously 
contributed technical expertise, and a flag flies at half mast on the ANZAC Bridge in 
Sydney.  
We thank all of those who have worked so hard on the attempted rescue of these 
men. From the moment of the first expl osion, they have spent every waking hour 
tirelessly working, searching for a way to bring these men home alive. We acknowledge 
their professionalism at a time of enormous  frustration. We also acknowledge all those 
who have given their time and energy to support the families. Much more will be asked 
of them in the days to come.  
The next step now is to make the mine as safe as possible, so that the men’s bodies 
can be recovered. It is also  natural and appropriate that New Zealanders are seeking 
answers to how this disaster occurred. Fam ilies want certainty about  the events leading 
up to their loved ones’ deaths, and we all need to know how such a disaster can be 
prevented in the future. Cabinet will confirm the details of a commission of inquiry at 
its next meeting on Monday, along with an y other inquiries th at may be deemed 
appropriate.  
Today we also acknowledge the sense of loss felt by all New Zealanders who have 
watched the story of the Pike River miners  unfold. Each passing day of this tragedy 
made the hopes and frustrations of the West  Coast community and the miners’ families 
our hopes and frustrations. These are me n whose names we did not know, but we 
instinctively recognised their qua lities collectively as the be st of ours. These were men 
15808 Motions 25 Nov 2010 
who knew the strain and satis faction of physical work, a nd who lived in a community 
where teamwork, hard work, and practical skill are respected. They were breadwinners 
for their families and earners for their community. They died not fighting a war in a 
strange land, nor taking undue risks; they di ed, shockingly, going to work. They were 
ordinary people who died in extraordinary and perhaps horrible circumstances. Their 
numbers are no consolation to the grief of each  individual family. That is the pain of 
each family alone. But the scale and the horror of this tragedy have dragged us all to the 
entrance of the Pike River mine, and today we stand there together with the families and 
the West Coast community, contemplating wh at might have happened in the darkness. 
Who among us did not hope that the qualities of these men, which we regard as the best 
of our own qualities, would tr iumph over the odds and lead them into the light? It was 
not to be.  
As the tragedy passes, it is our hope that  the families and communities can be held 
together by the toughness, the comradeship, the resilience, and the commitment to the 
common good that we all share with those w ho are lost. The darkness took their lives, 
but it cannot take the love th at these men had for their families and their mates, and nor 
can it take our respect for them. May they rest in peace.  
Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) : The Labour Opposition joins 
all parties in this House in sending our sympathy to the families and friends of the 29 
men who perished in the Pike River Coal mi ne disaster yesterday. We are also thinking 
of the people of the West Coast who have woke n this morning to the reality of the loss, 
knowing that all hope of life has been extinguished. 
Not a day goes by that we do not hear or read of a tragedy somewhere in the world 
from natural or human causes—earthquakes to floods, famine to fire—and we watch the 
passing parade of pictures on our television sets . We feel sad at their loss and we shake 
our heads at the enormity of their tragedy, but nothing hurts like the death of your own. 
Twenty-nine men have died, and although fi ve of them are from other countries—
Scotland, Australia, and South Africa—they now lie alongside our men and they too are 
now New Zealanders. 
There will be very few people in New Zealand today who do not feel a sense of loss 
and deep sadness as we look at  the faces of the family members, the rescuers, the 
community leaders, and the clergy, all grief-stri cken at their loss and frustrated at their 
inability to save those lives. As the headlin es in our newspaper said today, it is “Our 
darkest hour”. So many words have already be en said and written over the past 6 days, 
and no doubt many more will follow. Eventuall y, the stories of this  tragedy will also 
become part of the West Coast legend. 
On Friday the Mayor of Grey District, Tony Kokshoorn, who has shown incredible 
leadership, said that there was a little bit of the West Coast in all of us. I think he is 
right. But there is a little bit of the coalmine r in many of us, as well. My old dad started 
his working life at 14 years of age in the Owen River mine, 13 miles north of 
Murchison. His dad worked in the mine, t oo. And his dad before him worked in the 
Denniston mine, where he broke his back in a mining accident. And his dad was a miner 
from Jarrow, County Durham, who came to New Zealand for a better life—and my 
generation got that better life. That will be a familiar story for thousands of New 
Zealanders whose family grew out of a mi ning tradition on the We st Coast, or in 
Southland, Huntly, or Waihī. 
When most of us think of working in a coalmine, we think of dirt and dust and 
darkness, hard labour, and da nger. But for those who go down  the mines it is a way of 
life. Few other jobs build the sense of brotherhood and loyalty to each other that miners 
have. The West Coast reputati on of stoic, strong fighters ar ises out of that mining 
tradition. Now all that strength of character and fighting spirit are going to be needed in 
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15809 
the days ahead. As John Crowley, a West Coaster writing in the Dominion Post  said 
today, “what will tomorrow bring … It will br ing a heavy blanket of abject sadness.”, 
until the region rises again from  this devastating experience. It will rise again, and they 
will not be alone. 
This morning I was talking to Rick Barker. He is a boy from Rūnanga, who has spent 
the last 5 days in Greymouth. He said what a close-knit commun ity it is. In one street in 
Rūnanga, Ranfurly Street, two grieving mothers live just a short distance apart. Many 
others in that street are connected to the mi ners who died. Rick sa id there have been 5 
days of dread, 5 days of hope, 5 days of c ourage, and 5 days of great leadership, but 
now is the time to mourn, and to focus on retrieving the bodies of the men so that there 
can be closure for their families. Then there will be a time to find out what went wrong. 
May they rest in peace. 
KEVIN HAGUE (Green) : A speech like this is normally given by one of our co-
leaders, and I want to begin by expressing my thanks to Metiria and Russel for giving 
me the opportunity to speak on this tragedy today and to express our profound sorrow. I 
live the closest to the mine of anyone in this Parliament. When I spoke earl ier this week 
about every family and every household in and around Greymouth being connected to at 
least one of the men who is trapped in the mine, I include my own in that. One of my 
partner’s relations was killed in the Strongm an Mine disaster in 1967. That tragedy has 
echoed down the years, through our family and through the community. Now the name 
of Pike River joins that te rrible toll of Strongman, Dobson, Brunner, and many other 
disasters. Those who were bereaved by these previous disasters will feel afresh their 
own pain but will also know best of all the anguish a nd grief now being experienced by 
the families and friends of the 29 men killed.  
When I spoke on Tuesday I expressed the fervent hope that the men would be 
brought home. That is still my fervent hope . Families need the bodies of their loved 
ones to come home so that they may prope rly grieve, and I know that that is well 
understood and that no effort will be spared, nor should it, to do this.  
I want to again express my and the Green Party’s sincerest thanks and admiration for 
the work done by Tony Kokshoorn, Gary Know les and the police, the other emergency 
services and Mines Rescue, the district he alth board and its staff, the New Zealand 
Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union, the Red Cross, the 
churches of Greymouth, and everyone else who has been involved in providing support. 
I want to express my personal gratitude to  other members of this House—those who 
have been helping out directly on the Coast, but also everyone else. I feel that when I 
return home this afternoon, I will be carrying with me the support and well-wishes of 
this whole House. I will single out Peter Whittall. I know Peter pe rsonally, but I will 
take this public opportunity  to convey the Green Part y’s thanks, our enormous 
sympathy, but also our tremendous respec t for the integrity, responsibility, and 
compassion that he has unfailingly shown. I am sure that that is a feeling shared by the 
nation.  
There is a memorial to those lost in the Brunner Mine disast er in the road leading out 
of Greymouth up towards Pike River. It carries an inscription from the New Zealand 
Tablet from 3 April 1896: “While the wido ws and orphans were watching with 
heartbroken anxiety at the pit mouth for the result of the rescue work, all New Zealand 
seemed to stand by and share the grief of the bereaved ones.” This is a loss being felt by 
a whole country. When we consider the deva station and emptiness that we feel, we 
know that this is nothing compared with the utter loss suffered by the bereaved families. 
Our hearts go out to you. If we could shar e your burden, we would do it, but we cannot. 
We will sup
port you in any way that we can, and we will remember them. 
15810 Motions 25 Nov 2010 
Hon RODNEY HIDE (Leader—ACT) : It is with deep and overwhelming sadness 
that I rise today on behalf of the ACT Party to join with all members of this House to 
offer our heartfelt sympathy and our support to  the families and to the loved ones of the 
Pike River coalminers whose lives have b een so tragically taken away. Words cannot 
even begin to express the sorrow we f eel at the profound loss of 29 good men, who 
were loved by their community and by their fa milies. We are also well aware that the 
deep sorrow that we feel now is only a frac tion of that being experienced on the West 
Coast. 
The people of Greymouth possess an immense strength of characte r. We have seen 
your courage and your determination time and time again. We have seen you face 
adversity head on. The days to come will be  incredibly difficult , both emotionally and 
physically, but we know that you will come  through this and your community will 
become stronger. 
All New Zealanders are united in grief today and will never ever forget the loss of 
these 29 miners. These men were part of the backbone of New Zealand: family men, 
working men; men who kissed their wives, their parents, and th eir children goodbye as 
they left for work on Friday, never once imagining that they would not be coming 
home. I cannot begin to comprehend how those families must be feeling right now. 
I too wish to thank the entire rescue t eam and all those who offered assistance, 
advice, support, and expertise. We know that  there is still much work to be done, but 
your efforts will be of invaluable assistance and comfort in this time of need. 
I say thank you to Peter Whittall, Chief Executive of Pike River Coal. Thank you for 
your leadership, your courage, your honest y, and your humanity. I know that all New 
Zealanders will continue to support you and all your staff in the days and weeks ahead. I 
know that the job and the decisions you have ahead of you to ensure that Pike River 
Coal remains on the West Coast, and to ensure the employment of miners and staff, will 
be difficult but it is of critical importance. 
As Minister of Local Government, let me  pay tribute to councillor Milton John 
Osborne, 54, of Ng āhere, who was one of the 29 in th e mine at the time of Friday’s 
explosion. Milton was serving his second te rm on the Grey District Council as a 
representative for the eastern ward where he was elected unopposed. He was also a 
contractor at the Pike River mine. Grey District Council Chief Executive, Paul 
Pretorius, said that Milton was highly respected for his council work. He took a wide 
interest in council issues. Th e area he represented was very close to him. Milton had a 
special concern for the farming issues in Ng āhere, and he represen ted the farmers with 
conviction. Milton always looked at the merits  of each case and carefully considered 
things, always coming very well prepared to council meetings. His input was ever 
thoughtful and he also included the lighter side, while always making perfect sense. 
Milton was a big friendly guy with a great se nse of humour. He could come up with a 
joke at the most appropriate and, indeed, th e most inappropriate times. He lived his life 
without apology. He was a caring father and a good husband. He and his wife were 
great friends. He was respected, he was valu ed, and he was loved as a member of the 
council. I would like to quote Paul’s fina l comment verbatim: “Milton epitomises the 
West Coast: he was a good bastard.” 
I also wish to acknowledge  and thank the Mayor of Greymouth, Tony Kokshoorn, 
who has been the face of the community dur ing this difficult and gut-wrenching time. 
Tony’s courage, support, and leadership gave strength to the families and friends who 
live in this close-knit community. I offer you my support and strength. 
As Associate Minister of Education, I also  recognise the work of the Ministry of 
Education’s traumatic incident team. The team has worked ti relessly to support staff in 
25 Nov 2010 Motions 15811 
schools and early childhood education services in the area so that children can maintain 
the rhythm of their lives during a time of great uncertainty and sorrow. 
Mining is a way of life on the West Coast,  and in Greymouth especially. For many 
families, mining is more than just a liveli hood; it is a tradition. On e could say it is in 
their blood. It is for this reason that we cannot allow mining to cease on the West Coast; 
rather we must find out how this happened a nd we must see what lessons we can learn 
from it. Although it is difficult today to see beyond the sorrow, may looking back in 
memory help comfort you tomorrow. Rest in peace. God bless their souls. 
Hon JIM ANDERTON (Leader—Progressive) : Like all New Zealanders, I am 
deeply saddened by the loss of the 29 mi ners in Greymouth, and my thoughts and 
prayers are with the loved ones who are left behind.  
As a nation, and as a House I am sure, we have clung on to a glimmer of hope in the 
past 6 days. With every passing hour we ha ve put our faith in the possibility of a 
miracle. Fears over entering the mine safely, which had been such a concern to 
Superintendent Gary Knowles, were well justified when th e second explosion occurred 
yesterday. He and Pike River Coal Chief Executive Peter Whittall have shown calm, 
intelligent leadership and great strength at a difficult time. No praise is high enough for 
all of those who were part of the plans to secure the rescue of these men. Hope, 
however, for the 29 men trapped down the Pi ke River mine disappeared yesterday 
afternoon.  
This event has, of course, been a tragedy for the West Coast and its community and, 
needless to say, for the whole of New Zeala nd. It brought back some sad memories to 
many who have, unfortunately, been in this space before. Mining is an iconic industry 
on the West Coast, but that does not mean, however, that the rest of us have no 
responsibility for ensuring that such a tragedy does not happen again. We must refuse to 
accept that any of the deaths are a necessary cost of mining. It is a responsibility of all 
of us, from mine operators to  the Government and this Parliament, to take steps to 
strengthen mine safety so that the safety of all our miners is our No. 1 concern.  
Pike River is a modern, state-of-the-art mine with, presumably, all of the latest safety 
technology. But that did not sa ve the lives of the 29 men we lost yesterday. The new 
mine was on the same coal seam as the mine in Brunner where 65 men were killed by 
choking gas in 1896. It echoed th e Strongman mine explosion, which killed 19 miners 
in 1967. And there have been, even as recently as last year, many other similar disasters 
in other countries. How many more deaths mu st we experience in this industry before 
we ask some very serious questions about the vi ability of this type of mine? It will be 
the best possible tribute to those who di ed if we carefully examine the most 
comprehensive safety measures possible before we put any more miners in harm’s way.  
Since colonisation, the West Coast has had a long history in mining. The risk of 
mining has always been faced by miners and, as  a consequence, their families. Today is 
a time to reflect on the human tragedy of th is latest mining disast er, but these precious 
lost lives must be treasured th rough the efforts of all of us to see that this kind of 
catastrophe does not occur again. 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader—United Future) : There are, thankfully, only a few 
awful tragedies in the life of a nation that ar e so powerful in their impact, so searing on 
the emotions, that we all stop still, frozen in time as it were for that moment, and reflect 
upon what has happened, what its impact is going to be, and what its impact on us as a 
nation has been. Although it would be infelicitous to make comparisons, I can think of a 
few in my own lifetime to which the tragic events at Pike River must now be added. It is 
not just, awful as it is, the death of 29 mine rs in horrific circumstances; this was an 
event that stopped a nation. We all felt fo r those miners—desperately—and even more 
so for their families and loved ones, their friends, their neighb ours, and their colleagues. 
15812 Motions 25 Nov 2010 
Every time Peter Whittall appeared on television to provide an update we could see and 
feel his pain and his genuine sense of wanti ng desperately to bring those men out alive, 
and we were with him. Yesterday’s events dashed whatever remaining hopes there were 
in that regard, and now a country, a region, and individual families deal with the 
consequences.  
I guess that for those families there will be the awful shock of adjusting to what has 
happened. There will be the consolation of a tight-knit community and the love of a 
nation all around them. But, sadly, that is passing. Once the memorial services have 
been held, and once life starts to pick up its inevitable threads again, their pain will 
endure and their grief will carry on. The r eal challenge for all of us in this 
compassionate society is about their ongoing support and their ongoing place in our 
collective heart, as we struggle to overcome the consequences of this tragedy.  
It bites deep. It is not just a case of thinking about th e West Coast and what has 
happened there. Earlier this morning I was vi siting Inland Revenue Department staff in 
Christchurch, partly in the wake of the events that they have suffered following the 
Christchurch earthquake, only to be inform ed that one of the staff members in 
Christchurch is the mother of one of thos e lost in the mine. So we have people who 
have gone through a different set of em otions, following an earthquake, coming 
together to get over those, to now be faced with another tragedy in their midst. This 
must surely be New Zealand’s annus horribilis.  
At this time our words are inadequate, however well meant, and our gestures, 
however well meant, will not be  enough. Our challeng e as a people as we stand still so 
numbed by this shock, so awestruck by what  has happened, is to never forget those 
families, to do what we can to assist them materially and otherwise right now and into 
the future, and to pay them the ultimate c ourtesy of finding out what happened, what 
lessons can be learnt, and what steps can be taken to prevent any form of repetition at a 
future date.  
Much has been said about the heart a nd soul of the miners, and I acknowledge 
particularly the comments from my collea gue Mr Hide regarding Milton Osborne, who 
as I said the other day had been a candi date for United Future at the 2005 general 
election. I acknowledge the stor ies we are hearing about so  many of the other miners—
their contributions to life well beyond their working careers, to their families, their 
communities, and their sports . I acknowledge also the hopes that are now diminished 
and will never be achieved, and the aspirations unmet.  
This is an occasion where we all figurative ly want to give those suffering people one 
giant hug of support. I suppose the only thing we can now hope for is that the bodies are 
recovered quickly, that there can be closur e through the memorial services, and that 
those who suffered and died so unnecessarily can at last rest in peace. 
TE URUROA FLAVELL (M āori Party—Waiariki): Whakataka te hau ki te uru, 
whakataka te hau ki te tonga, kia mākinakina ki uta, kia mātaratara ki tai. Kia hī ake ana 
te atākura, he tio, he huka, he hauhunga. Tihe—e mauri ora! 
E te parekura, e ng ā mate, e ng ā aituā o te w ā, e ngā tōtara nui o te wao, koutou kua 
tangohia e te Ringa-Kaha-o-Aitu ā,
